yanhuitlan.t: An important Mixtec kingdom of the Mixteca Alta, known for its rich colonial records and its great Dominican church.
yanhuitlan.o: Yanhuitlan, Yodzo Cahi in Mixtec, emerged as a significant kingdom in the fertile Nochixtlán valley in the Postclassic period, from around 1200, and became one of the most populous Mixtec states.
yanhuitlan.r: It was ruled by a hereditary lord and lady drawn from the intermarried Mixtec nobility. Like its neighbours, it was organised into a royal household, nobles and dependent commoners, and produced cochineal, textiles and fine crafts. It was made a tributary of the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] in the late 15th century.
yanhuitlan.e: Yanhuitlan came under Spanish rule around 1522. The [[e:portuguese-inquisition|Inquisition]] trial of its native lords in 1544-46 for practising traditional religion is a key source on Mixtec society. The vast 16th-century Dominican church of Santo Domingo still dominates the town.

yuwen-xianbei.t: A Xianbei confederation of the upper Liao River destroyed by the Murong in 344, whose descendants later founded the Northern Zhou dynasty.
yuwen-xianbei.o: The Yuwen ruling house was said to be of [[s:southern-xiongnu|Southern Xiongnu]] origin and became leaders of a Xianbei-speaking confederation in the Shira Muren valley of eastern Inner [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]] in the late 3rd century, with its centre at Zixiong.
yuwen-xianbei.r: The Yuwen were mounted herders and hunters ruled by hereditary chiefs. They were the main rivals of the Murong [[s:xianbei|Xianbei]] to the south-east and allies at times of [[s:later-zhao|Later Zhao]]. Chinese sources describe them as fierce but loosely organised.
yuwen-xianbei.e: In 344 Murong [[s:state-of-huang|Huang]] of [[s:former-yan|Former Yan]] defeated the chief Yuwen Yidougui, who fled and died in the steppe, and over 50,000 households were moved south. Yuwen descendants rose again two centuries later: Yuwen Tai dominated [[s:western-wei|Western Wei]] and his family founded the [[s:northern-zhou|Northern Zhou]]. The Kumo Xi and Khitan were said to descend from Yuwen remnants.

yehud-medinata.t: Yehud Medinata, the small Persian province of Judah centred on Jerusalem's rebuilt temple, where Second Temple Judaism took shape.
yehud-medinata.o: After Cyrus of the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] conquered [[e:babylon|Babylon]] in 539 BCE, Judaean exiles were allowed to return to [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]]. The province of Yehud was formed in the hills around the city, and under the governor Zerubbabel the [[e:temple-in-jerusalem|Second Temple]] was completed c. 515 BCE.
yehud-medinata.r: Persian-appointed governors and the high priests of the temple shared authority. Nehemiah, a court official, rebuilt [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem's]] walls c. 445 BCE, and Ezra brought the law of Moses to the centre of community life. The province minted small [[e:silver|silver]] coins inscribed Yehud and used [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]] for administration.
yehud-medinata.e: Yehud passed peacefully to Alexander of the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] in 332 BCE and then to the [[s:ptolemaic-empire|Ptolemaic Empire]] and the [[s:seleucid-empire|Seleucid Empire]]. The texts and institutions shaped there formed the basis of later [[e:judaism|Judaism]].

yogyakarta-sultanate.t: Javanese sultanate created by the division of Mataram in 1755, which backed Indonesian independence and still rules its city as a special region.
yogyakarta-sultanate.o: The Treaty of Giyanti of 1755, brokered by the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]], ended a long succession war by splitting the [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram Sultanate]] in two. Prince Mangkubumi received the western half and became [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Hamengkubuwono I, building a new kraton at Yogyakarta, while the eastern half became the [[s:surakarta-sunanate|Surakarta Sunanate]].
yogyakarta-sultanate.r: The sultan ruled as a Muslim king and heir to Javanese kingship, with an elaborate court culture of gamelan, wayang, dance and batik. Royal lands supported nobles through apanages. British troops sacked the kraton in 1812, and the Yogyakarta prince Diponegoro led the [[e:java|Java]] War against the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] from 1825 to 1830. [[s:pakualaman|Pakualaman]] was carved from it in 1812.
yogyakarta-sultanate.e: [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Hamengkubuwono IX sided with the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]], which made Yogyakarta its capital from 1946 to 1949. It became a Special Region in 1950, and a 2012 law confirmed that the reigning sultan serves as its governor. Hamengkubuwono X reigns today.

yabghus-of-tokharistan.t: A Turkic dynasty that ruled Tokharistan, the old Bactria, from Kunduz, holding together a patchwork of principalities between the Turks, Tang China and the Arabs.
yabghus-of-tokharistan.o: After the [[s:western-turkic-khaganate|Western Turkic Khaganate]] took [[s:greco-bactrian-kingdom|Bactria]] from the [[s:hephthalite-empire|Hephthalites]], Tong Yabghu [[e:khagan|Khagan]] installed his son Tardu Shad as yabghu, or [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]], of Tokharistan around 625, with his seat at Kunduz. Xuanzang met Tardu Shad there shortly before he was poisoned.
yabghus-of-tokharistan.r: The yabghus were overlords of some 27 local principalities, including [[s:principality-of-khuttal|Khuttal]], Chaghaniyan and Bamiyan, many ruled by Hephthalite dynasties. [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] flourished, with great monasteries at Balkh and Bamiyan. Under [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China's]] [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] system the yabghus received Chinese titles and sent embassies asking for help against the [[e:arabs|Arabs]], who took Balkh and pressed into the region from the 650s.
yabghus-of-tokharistan.e: The yabghus became [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[e:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyads]], and in 709 to 710 the Hephthalite prince Nizak Tarkhan, who held the yabghu in his custody, led a revolt crushed by Qutayba ibn Muslim. The dynasty survived as Abbasid clients, with records of envoys to [[e:china|China]] until about 758, after which Tokharistan was absorbed into Islamic Khurasan.

yemen-arab-republic.t: North Yemen's republic, born in the 1962 revolution against the imamate, which fought a long civil war before uniting with the South in 1990.
yemen-arab-republic.o: On 26 September 1962 army officers led by Abdullah al-Sallal overthrew [[e:imam|Imam]] Muhammad al-Badr of the [[s:mutawakkilite-kingdom-of-yemen|Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen]] and proclaimed the [[e:yemen|Yemen]] Arab Republic. [[e:egypt|Egypt]] sent tens of thousands of troops to defend it, while [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]] backed the royalists.
yemen-arab-republic.r: The civil war lasted until 1970, when [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]] recognised the republic. Politics remained dominated by army officers and tribal leaders of the Hashid and Bakil confederations. President Ibrahim al-Hamdi was assassinated in 1977, and his successor too, before Ali Abdullah Saleh took power in 1978. Remittances from workers in Saudi [[e:arabia|Arabia]] sustained the economy, and oil was found near Marib in 1984.
yemen-arab-republic.e: After border wars in 1972 and 1979 and years of talks, North [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] united with [[s:south-yemen|South Yemen]] on 22 May 1990 to form the Republic of [[e:yemen|Yemen]], with Saleh as president.

yarkent-khanate.t: A Chagatai khanate of the western Tarim Basin, ruled from Yarkand, whose khans patronised poetry and Sufi orders until the Dzungars conquered it.
yarkent-khanate.o: In 1514 [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Said Khan, a descendant of Yunus Khan of [[s:moghulistan|Moghulistan]], took [[s:kingdom-of-shule|Kashgar]] and Yarkand from the [[e:dughlat|Dughlat]] amir Mirza Aba Bakr, founding a khanate with Yarkand as its capital. His cousin Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat, author of the Tarikh-i Rashidi, served at his court.
yarkent-khanate.r: The khans ruled the oasis towns of [[s:kingdom-of-shule|Kashgar]], Yarkand, [[s:kingdom-of-khotan|Khotan]] and Aksu, with an agricultural economy and caravan trade to [[e:india|India]] and [[e:china|China]]. Under Abd al-Rashid Khan the court was a centre of music, and his queen Amannisa Khan is credited with compiling the [[e:uyghurs|Uyghur]] Muqam. In the 17th century the Naqshbandi Khoja families, divided into Aqtaghliq and Qarataghliq factions, became increasingly powerful.
yarkent-khanate.e: In 1680 the Aqtaghliq leader Afaq Khoja invited the [[s:dzungar-khanate|Dzungar Khanate]] under Galdan Boshugtu, which conquered the khanate. The Khojas ruled as [[e:dzungars|Dzungar]] [[e:vassal|vassals]] until the Chagatai line was formally ended around 1705.

yaxha.t: A Classic Maya city on the shore of Lake Yaxha in north-eastern Petén, a long-time rival of nearby Naranjo.
yaxha.o: Yaxha, one of the few Maya cities whose ancient name survives, grew on a ridge above Lake Yaxha from the Preclassic period. By the Early Classic it was a substantial city with its own emblem glyph and plazas laid out in Tikal-related styles.
yaxha.r: The city had more than 500 structures, including acropolis complexes, twin-pyramid groups like those at [[s:tikal|Tikal]], and causeways leading to the lakeshore. Its rulers fought frequently with [[s:naranjo|Naranjo]]: in 710 Naranjo's king K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Chaak claimed a victory over Yaxha and the scattering of a former Yaxha king's bones, and Naranjo attacked again in 799.
yaxha.e: Yaxha declined around 800 CE and was abandoned soon after, though smaller settlements persisted on lake islands into the Postclassic. It is now part of the Yaxha-Nakum-Naranjo National Park.

yelang.t: The largest kingdom of the south-western peoples in Guizhou, remembered for a king who asked a Han envoy whether Han was larger than Yelang.
yelang.o: Yelang was a polity of the south-western peoples in western Guizhou and neighbouring Yunnan and Guangxi, emerging in the late Warring States period. It controlled the Zangke River route down to the Pearl River and the lands of [[s:nanyue|Nanyue]].
yelang.r: The Records of the Grand Historian describe Yelang as a settled kingdom of farmers with walled towns. Han envoys reached it in 135 BCE seeking a route to [[s:nanyue|Nanyue]], and the marquis Duotong accepted Han titles. Its ruler's question to the envoys about which state was larger gave rise to the Chinese idiom for self-importance born of ignorance.
yelang.e: After the [[s:han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] conquered [[s:nanyue|Nanyue]] in 111 BCE, Yelang submitted and its ruler received the title of king, while Han established Zangke [[e:commandery|Commandery]]. Around 27 BCE the Han governor Chen Li executed the king, Xing, for rebellion and the kingdom was abolished.

yamatai.t: The realm of Queen Himiko, the earliest Japanese state described in detail by Chinese historians, whose location is still one of Japan's great debates.
yamatai.o: The Chinese Records of the [[e:three-kingdoms-period|Three Kingdoms]] describe how the Wa people, after years of war in the late 2nd century, agreed to make Himiko their ruler. She reigned from Yamatai over about thirty polities. Scholars still dispute whether Yamatai lay in northern Kyushu or in the Nara basin, where the Makimuku site is a leading candidate.
yamatai.r: Himiko was said to practise sorcery and rarely appeared in public; her younger brother handled government. Subject countries paid taxes, markets were supervised, and officials inspected the coastal lands. In 239 she sent envoys to the Wei court and was named Queen of Wa Friendly to Wei, receiving a gold seal and bronze mirrors.
yamatai.e: After Himiko's death around 248, a king failed to keep order and the girl Iyo became ruler. The last recorded embassy reached [[e:china|China]] in 266, after which Yamatai vanishes from the sources; its relation to the [[s:yamato|Yamato polity]] is unclear.

yonezawa-domain.t: The Uesugi domain of Dewa, famous for the reforms of Uesugi Yozan, who rescued it from bankruptcy and became a model of benevolent rule.
yonezawa-domain.o: Uesugi Kagekatsu opposed [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] in 1600 and in 1601 was stripped of his vast Aizu fief, keeping only Yonezawa with 300,000 koku. The clan kept most of its retainers, leaving the domain burdened with a huge [[e:samurai|samurai]] class.
yonezawa-domain.r: In 1664 a succession irregularity halved the domain to 150,000 koku, and debts mounted. From 1767 Uesugi Harunori, known as Yozan, imposed frugality, encouraged [[e:sericulture|sericulture]], weaving, lacquer trees and carp ponds, reclaimed land and revived the Kojokan school, restoring the finances over decades. His maxim that if one tries, it can be done remains well known in [[e:japan|Japan]].
yonezawa-domain.e: Yonezawa joined the [[s:ouetsu-reppan-domei|Ouetsu Reppan Domei]] in 1868 and surrendered that autumn. After abolition in 1871 it became part of Yamagata Prefecture.

yapese-chiefdoms.t: The ranked village chiefdoms of Yap in Micronesia, known for giant stone money and the sawei system that bound distant atolls to the district of Gagil.
yapese-chiefdoms.o: Yap, a cluster of high islands in the western Caroline Islands, was settled over 2,000 years ago. By the time of European contact its villages had been arranged in a strict ranking, with three paramount villages heading rival alliances. Gachpar in the district of Gagil led the network of outer islands, a relationship known as the sawei.
yapese-chiefdoms.r: Land, not persons, carried rank on Yap: each estate held a title, and chiefs of high villages commanded the services of low-[[e:caste|caste]] villages. Through the sawei, atolls from Ulithi to Namonuito sent cloth, mats and shell valuables to Gagil, receiving food and protection against typhoons and sorcery in return. Yapese voyagers quarried huge limestone discs, rai, in Palau and carried them home as stone money, still used in ceremonial exchange. Taro swamps and fishing supported the population.
yapese-chiefdoms.e: A dispute between [[e:spain|Spain]] and [[e:germany|Germany]] over Yap in 1885 was settled by [[e:papacy|Pope]] Leo XIII in Spain's favour, and Spanish rule began in 1886. Germany, [[e:japan|Japan]] and the [[s:united-states|United States]] followed. Yap is now a state of the Federated States of Micronesia, where chiefly councils keep a constitutional role.

yamato.t: The early Japanese kingship of the Nara basin that built giant keyhole tombs, adopted Buddhism and laid the foundations of the Japanese imperial state.
yamato.o: From the mid-3rd century huge keyhole-shaped burial mounds appeared in the Nara basin, marking a confederation of chiefs led by a great king, or okimi. By the 5th century Yamato rulers, recorded in [[e:china|China]] as the five kings of Wa, controlled much of western [[e:japan|Japan]]; an inscribed sword from Inariyama names King Wakatakeru, usually identified as Yuryaku.
yamato.r: Power rested on hereditary clans (uji) ranked by titles and bound to the court, with specialist groups of craftsmen, many of Korean origin. [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] arrived from [[s:baekje|Baekje]] in the 6th century and was championed by the Soga clan. Prince Shotoku issued a seventeen-article code in 604, and the Taika reforms of 645 began a centralised land and tax system on Chinese lines.
yamato.e: Defeat at Baekgang in 663 and the Jinshin war of 672 led Tenmu and his successors to build a bureaucratic state. The Taiho code of 701 completed the transition to [[s:ritsuryo-japan|Ritsuryo Japan]].

yaxchilan.t: A Classic Maya kingdom in a loop of the Usumacinta river, celebrated for its carved lintels showing royal bloodletting and the reigns of the Shield Jaguar kings.
yaxchilan.o: Yaxchilan, anciently Pa' Chan, occupied a defensible bend of the Usumacinta on today's Mexico-[[e:guatemala|Guatemala]] border. Its dynasty traced descent from Yopaat B'ahlam I, who took power in 359 CE, and early rulers fought repeatedly with neighbouring [[s:piedras-negras|Piedras Negras]] for control of the river.
yaxchilan.r: Its greatest age came under Itzamnaaj B'ahlam (Shield Jaguar), who reigned from 681 to 742, and his son Yaxuun B'ahlam IV (Bird Jaguar). Lintels 24 to 26, commissioned for Lady K'ab'al Xook, show a royal woman drawing blood from her tongue and conjuring a vision serpent. Temples and palaces were set on terraces above the river, and its kings dominated nearby [[s:bonampak|Bonampak]].
yaxchilan.e: The last known ruler, K'inich Tatbu Skull IV, is recorded around 808, and the city was abandoned soon after. Its lintels, some now in the [[e:british-museum|British Museum]], are among the finest Maya reliefs.

yawnghwe-state.t: The Shan state of Inle Lake, whose last ruler, Sao Shwe Thaike, became the first president of independent Burma.
yawnghwe-state.o: Yawnghwe, Burmese Nyaungshwe, lay at the northern end of Inle Lake in the southern Shan plateau. Shan tradition dates its ruling house to 1359, when two brothers are said to have settled the area with Burmese royal approval. It became one of the leading southern Shan states.
yawnghwe-state.r: Its saophas ruled a lake and valley economy of floating gardens, [[e:rice|rice]] and fishing worked by Intha, Shan, Pa-O and Danu peoples. The Phaung Daw Oo pagoda on the lake, with its five Buddha images carried in an annual boat procession, was a major centre of devotion. Yawnghwe paid tribute to Ava and later to the Konbaung kings.
yawnghwe-state.e: Under British rule Yawnghwe became part of the [[s:federated-shan-states|Federated Shan States]]. Sao Shwe Thaike, its saopha, served as the first President of the [[s:myanmar|Union of Burma]] from 1948 to 1952. The rulers renounced their powers in 1959, and Sao Shwe Thaike died in prison after the 1962 coup.

yemen-vilayet.t: The second Ottoman province of Yemen, held against constant Zaydi revolts until the empire's defeat in 1918.
yemen-vilayet.o: The [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] returned to [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] in 1849, occupying the coastal Tihama and Hodeidah. After the opening of the Suez Canal increased the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea's]] value, Ahmed Muhtar Pasha led an expedition that took Sanaa in 1872, ending the [[s:qasimid-state|Qasimid State]]'s last remnant and creating the [[e:yemen|Yemen]] Vilayet.
yemen-vilayet.r: The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] introduced [[e:telegraph|telegraphs]], schools and courts and drew a border with the [[s:aden-settlement|British Aden]] [[e:protectorate|Protectorate]] in 1904-1914. Taxation and [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] law provoked repeated Zaydi risings: [[e:imam|Imam]] al-Mansur Muhammad and from 1904 his son Imam Yahya besieged Sanaa, and Ottoman losses were heavy. The Treaty of Da'an in 1911 gave Yahya authority over the Zaydi highlands under Ottoman [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]].
yemen-vilayet.e: Yahya stayed loyal during the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]]. After the [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|armistice]] of 1918 the Ottoman garrisons withdrew and he took Sanaa, founding the [[s:mutawakkilite-kingdom-of-yemen|Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen]]; the coast and the [[s:idrisid-emirate-of-asir|Idrisid Emirate of Asir]] followed different paths.

yaudheya-republic.t: A long-lived warrior republic of Haryana and Rajasthan that worshipped the war god Karttikeya and defied Saka and Kushan rulers.
yaudheya-republic.o: The Yaudheyas were already known to the grammarian Panini as a people who lived by arms. After the fall of the [[s:maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]] they emerged as an independent republic in the 2nd century BCE, holding land between the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] and the Yamuna in modern Haryana, [[e:punjab|Punjab]] and northern Rajasthan. Coin moulds found at Rohtak suggest it was an important centre.
yaudheya-republic.r: The Yaudheyas were a gana governed by an assembly and an elected leader. Their coins carry the legend Yaudheya ganasya jaya, victory to the Yaudheya republic, and images of Karttikeya, the war god they treated as their divine sovereign. Their reputation for military skill was such that the [[s:saka|Saka]] ruler Rudradaman boasted in his [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]] inscription of 150 of having defeated them.
yaudheya-republic.e: The Yaudheyas reasserted their independence after the decline of the [[s:kushan-empire|Kushan Empire]] in the 3rd century. In the 4th century they submitted to [[e:samudragupta|Samudragupta]] of the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]], whose Allahabad pillar inscription lists them, and they then disappear from history.

yan-five-dynasties.t: A brief empire proclaimed at Youzhou, near modern Beijing, by the warlord Liu Shouguang, crushed within two years by Jin.
yan-five-dynasties.o: Liu Rengong was military governor of Lulong, centred on Youzhou, in the late [[s:later-tang|Tang]]. In 907 his son Liu Shouguang imprisoned him and seized the province. In 911, after declining offers from the [[s:later-liang|Later Liang]], Liu Shouguang proclaimed himself emperor of [[s:yan-an-shi-rebellion|Great Yan]].
yan-five-dynasties.r: Sources portray Liu Shouguang as arrogant and cruel, ruling by fear and heavy taxation. The state held the north-eastern frontier, bordering the rising Khitan of the future [[s:liao-dynasty|Liao dynasty]], but had little support among its officials or neighbours.
yan-five-dynasties.e: Li Cunxu of [[s:jin-five-dynasties|Jin (Five Dynasties)]] sent his general Zhou Dewei against Yan in 911. Youzhou fell in 913, and Liu Shouguang was captured and executed in 914, and his father was also put to death. Yan's territory became part of Jin and later of the [[s:later-tang|Later Tang]].

yettishar.t: The Kashgarian state of Yaqub Beg, created during the Muslim revolts against the Qing and recognised by Britain, Russia and the Ottomans.
yettishar.o: During the uprising against Qing rule in [[e:xinjiang|Xinjiang]] from 1864, Kashgar's rebels invited the Khoja Buzurg Khan from [[e:kokand|Kokand]], accompanied by his general Yaqub Beg. Yaqub Beg soon sidelined Buzurg Khan, conquered [[s:kingdom-of-shule|Kashgar]], Yarkand and [[s:kingdom-of-khotan|Khotan]], and by 1870 controlled most of the [[e:tarim-basin|Tarim Basin]], including Turpan and Urumqi.
yettishar.r: Yettishar, 'seven cities', was ruled by Yaqub Beg as Atalik [[e:ghazi|Ghazi]], with an army trained along Ottoman lines and strict enforcement of Islamic law. He signed trade treaties with [[e:russia|Russia]] in 1872 and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1874, and the Ottoman sultan recognised him as emir. Heavy taxation and harsh rule caused resentment.
yettishar.e: The Qing general Zuo Zongtang reconquered [[e:xinjiang|Xinjiang]] from 1876. Yaqub Beg died at Korla in 1877, and his state collapsed. In 1884 the region became the Qing province of Xinjiang.

yueban.t: A nomad kingdom north of Kucha formed by Northern Xiongnu who stayed in Central Asia after the Han broke their power.
yueban.o: After Han [[e:china|China]] defeated the [[s:northern-xiongnu|Northern Xiongnu]] in the late 1st century CE, part of them fled west. According to the Book of Wei, those too weak to continue settled north of [[s:kingdom-of-kucha|Qiuci]] (Kucha), between the Tian Shan and the Tarbagatai, forming a state called Yueban in the 2nd century.
yueban.r: Chinese records describe a population of perhaps 200,000 who were cleaner in their habits than other [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]], washing and cutting their hair, and who sent envoys to the [[s:northern-wei|Northern Wei]] court in the 440s. Little else is known of its government or economy beyond its pastoral way of life.
yueban.e: Yueban was overrun by the [[s:rouran-khaganate|Rouran Khaganate]] and the Tiele in the late 5th century, and its people were absorbed into neighbouring steppe groups.

yufirid-dynasty.t: A highland Yemeni dynasty of the Himyarite tribe of Hiwal that held Sanaa and Shibam for over a century under nominal Abbasid rule.
yufirid-dynasty.o: Yu'fir ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Hiwali, from a Himyarite family, seized the highland fortress of Shibam Kawkaban around 847 and soon controlled Sanaa, ousting Abbasid governors while still naming the [[e:caliphate|caliph]] in [[e:khutba|Friday prayers]].
yufirid-dynasty.r: The Yufirids ruled a tribal highland state from Shibam and Sanaa, a rival to the [[s:ziyadid-dynasty|Ziyadid dynasty]] in the coastal Tihama. They faced the arrival of the Zaydi [[e:imam|imam]] al-Hadi in the north in 897 and the Isma'ili missionaries Ali ibn al-Fadl and Ibn Hawshab, who briefly captured Sanaa. As'ad ibn Ibrahim recovered the city and dominated highland politics in the early 10th century.
yufirid-dynasty.e: After As'ad's death in 944 the dynasty weakened through family feuds and tribal revolts. By about 997 it had lost Sanaa, and the highlands were contested between Zaydi [[e:imam|imams]], local chiefs and later the [[s:sulayhid-dynasty|Sulayhid dynasty]].

yemen-eyalet.t: The first Ottoman province of Yemen, conquered to fight the Portuguese and lost a century later to the Zaydi imams.
yemen-eyalet.o: In 1538 an [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] fleet under Hadim Suleiman Pasha, on its way to fight the Portuguese in [[e:india|India]], seized Aden and then Zabid. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] pushed into the highlands, taking Sanaa in 1547 under Ozdemir Pasha, and organised [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] as a province.
yemen-eyalet.r: Ottoman governors relied on garrisons and allied tribes and faced constant resistance from the [[s:zaydi-imamate-of-yemen|Zaydi Imamate of Yemen]]. A great revolt under al-Mutahhar in 1567 almost expelled them, until Sinan Pasha reconquered the country in 1569-1570. The province guarded the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]] approach to [[e:mecca|Mecca]], and the [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] trade through [[s:mohu|Mocha]] began to grow in this period.
yemen-eyalet.e: In 1597 al-Qasim ibn Muhammad began a new Zaydi revolt. His son al-Mu'ayyad Muhammad continued it, and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] left Sanaa and evacuated [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] in 1636, giving way to the [[s:qasimid-state|Qasimid State]].

yaaruba-dynasty.t: The Omani imamate that expelled the Portuguese from Oman and East Africa and turned Oman into the main naval power of the western Indian Ocean.
yaaruba-dynasty.o: In 1624 Ibadi scholars at Rustaq elected Nasir ibn Murshid al-Ya'rubi as [[e:imam|imam]], ending the rule of the [[s:nabhani-dynasty|Nabhani dynasty]]. He united the interior tribes and attacked the Portuguese coastal forts. His successor [[e:sultan|Sultan]] ibn Saif captured [[e:muscat|Muscat]] in 1650, ending [[s:portuguese-muscat|Portuguese Muscat]].
yaaruba-dynasty.r: The Ya'aruba built a navy and carried the war to [[e:east-africa|East Africa]], taking Fort Jesus at [[s:mombasa|Mombasa]] in 1698 under Saif ibn [[e:sultan|Sultan]] and gaining influence over [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]], Pemba and [[s:kilwa-sultanate|Kilwa]]. Trade in slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and dates enriched the state. The [[e:imam|imams]] built forts and palaces, including the round tower of Nizwa and the palace at Jabrin, and extended falaj irrigation.
yaaruba-dynasty.e: From 1718 disputed successions caused a civil war between the Hinawi and Ghafiri tribal factions, and one claimant invited Persian forces under [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]]. Ahmad ibn Said of Sohar expelled the [[e:persians|Persians]] and was elected [[e:imam|imam]] around 1744, founding the [[s:omani-empire|Omani Empire]] of the Al Bu Said.

yan-206-bc.t: The kingdom of Zang Tu in the Beijing region, created in 206 BCE, which switched sides to Liu Bang and was ended when its king rebelled against the new Han emperor.
yan-206-bc.o: Zang Tu was a general of the revived state of Yan who followed [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] to Julu and into the [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] heartland. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Yan, with his capital at Ji ([[e:beijing|Beijing]]), and moved the previous king, Han Guang, to Liaodong. Zang Tu killed Han Guang and took Liaodong as well.
yan-206-bc.r: Yan was a frontier kingdom facing the [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]] and the [[s:donghu|Donghu]], distant from the main [[e:theatre|theatres]] of the Chu-Han war. In 204 BCE, after Han Xin conquered Zhao, Zang Tu submitted to [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]] on the advice of the strategist Li Zuoche, without a battle.
yan-206-bc.e: Soon after [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]] proclaimed himself emperor in 202 BCE, Zang Tu rebelled. Liu Bang led the campaign himself, captured him and made his childhood friend Lu Wan King of Yan.

yuezhi.t: Nomads of the Gansu corridor who, driven west by the Xiongnu, conquered Bactria and gave rise to the Kushan Empire.
yuezhi.o: Chinese sources describe the Yuezhi as a powerful pastoral people between Dunhuang and the Qilian Mountains in the 3rd century BCE, strong enough to hold the young [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]] leader [[e:modu-chanyu|Modu]] as a hostage. Around 176 BCE the Xiongnu defeated them, and their king was later killed and his skull made into a drinking cup.
yuezhi.r: The main body, the Greater Yuezhi, migrated west through the Ili valley, displacing the [[s:saka|Saka]], then were pushed on by the [[s:wusun|Wusun]] to the [[e:oxus|Amu Darya]]. When the Han envoy Zhang Qian visited about 128 BCE they ruled [[s:greco-bactrian-kingdom|Bactria]] from north of the river, governing through five xihou or princely chiefdoms. Their identification with the Tocharian-speaking peoples is widely held but debated.
yuezhi.e: In the 1st century CE Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Guishuang (Kushan) branch, united the five chiefdoms and founded the [[s:kushan-empire|Kushan Empire]]. The Lesser Yuezhi who stayed behind in the Qilian Mountains merged with the Qiang peoples.

yiqu.t: A powerful Rong kingdom of the Loess Plateau that fought Qin for centuries, until a Qin queen dowager lured its king to his death in 272 BCE.
yiqu.o: The Yiqu were a Rong people of eastern Gansu and north-western Shaanxi, around modern Qingyang. By the 5th century BCE they had built walled towns and formed a kingdom strong enough to defeat the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]] in battle.
yiqu.r: The Yiqu combined farming with herding and controlled the uplands north of the Wei valley. Little is known of their institutions beyond Chinese accounts of wars and treaties with [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]]. Excavated tombs of the region show a mixture of steppe-style ornaments and Chinese bronzes.
yiqu.e: According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Queen Dowager Xuan of [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] had a liaison with the king of Yiqu and bore him two sons, then had him killed at the Ganquan palace in 272 BCE. Qin annexed his lands, created the Longxi, Beidi and [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] [[e:commandery|commanderies]] and built a long wall to protect them.

ychsma.t: A coastal lordship of the Rímac and Lurín valleys centred on Pachacamac, the most famous oracle and pilgrimage site of the ancient Andes.
ychsma.o: Ychsma, or Ichma, emerged around 1100 in the Lurín and lower Rímac valleys, where modern Lima stands, after the decline of Wari influence. It took over Pachacamac, a sacred site occupied since the time of the [[s:lima-culture|Lima culture]], and made it the heart of its territory.
ychsma.r: Ychsma was a group of lordships united around the cult of Pachacamac, the creator god whose oracle drew pilgrims from across the [[s:andecavi|Andes]]. Its lords built a series of pyramids with ramps at Pachacamac and other sites such as Armatambo and Mateo Salado. The economy relied on irrigation canals drawn from the Rímac and on fishing.
ychsma.e: The [[e:inca-empire|Incas]] absorbed Ychsma peacefully around 1470 and respected Pachacamac, adding a Temple of the Sun and an Acllahuasi. In 1533 Hernando Pizarro looted the temple. Spanish Lima was founded in Ychsma territory in 1535, and Pachacamac is now a major archaeological site.

yamhad.t: Yamhad, the Amorite great kingdom of Aleppo, which dominated northern Syria in the 18th and 17th centuries BCE until the Hittites destroyed it.
yamhad.o: Sumu-epuh founded the kingdom at Halab, modern [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], around 1810 BCE. He resisted Shamshi-Adad's [[s:kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia|Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia]], and his son Yarim-Lim I made Yamhad the leading power of [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]], allied with [[s:mari|Mari]] and [[e:babylon|Babylon]]; a [[e:mari|Mari]] letter claims twenty kings followed him.
yamhad.r: Its great kings ruled through dependent kingdoms such as [[s:kingdom-of-mukish|Alalakh]] in the Kingdom of Mukish and [[s:ebla|Ebla]], and their prestige rested on the temple of the storm god Hadad on the [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] citadel. Wealth came from the trade between the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] and the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]], and Hurrian culture spread widely among the elite.
yamhad.e: [[e:hattusili-i|Hattusili I]] of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] attacked Yamhad, and [[e:mursili-i|Mursili I]] destroyed [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] c. 1595 BCE. A reduced kingdom survived until the [[s:mitanni-empire|Mitanni Empire]] absorbed it in the 16th century BCE. The Aleppo storm-god temple remained venerated for centuries.

yan-an-shi-rebellion.t: The rebel empire of An Lushan and Shi Siming, whose eight-year war nearly destroyed the Tang and left China's north-east in the hands of warlords.
yan-an-shi-rebellion.o: [[e:an-lushan|An Lushan]], a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent and favourite of Emperor Xuanzong, commanded three frontier armies in the north-east. Fearing the chief minister Yang Guozhong, he rebelled at the end of 755, took [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] and early in 756 proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan, capturing [[e:changan|Chang'an]] that summer.
yan-an-shi-rebellion.r: The state was a military regime of frontier soldiers, including many Sogdian, Turkic and Khitan troops. It never governed securely: [[e:an-lushan|An Lushan]] was murdered by his son An Qingxu in 757, and [[s:later-tang|Tang]] forces, aided by [[e:uyghurs|Uyghur]] cavalry, retook both capitals that year. Shi Siming killed An Qingxu in 759, retook [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] and was in turn murdered by his son Shi Chaoyi in 761.
yan-an-shi-rebellion.e: Shi Chaoyi was defeated and killed himself in 763 as his generals surrendered. Millions had died or been displaced, and the [[s:tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] survived only by leaving the [[e:hebei|Hebei]] provinces to hereditary military governors, while the [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]] seized the north-west.

yopitzinco.t: A fiercely independent lordship of the Yopes (Tlapanecs) in the mountains of Guerrero, never subdued by the Aztec Empire.
yopitzinco.o: The Yopes lived in the rugged mountains and coast of eastern Guerrero, near modern [[e:acapulco|Acapulco]] and Ayutla. Their lordship, Yopitzinco, emerged in the Postclassic period, and is known mainly from Aztec and Spanish sources.
yopitzinco.r: Yopitzinco remained independent and was an enemy of the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]], which surrounded it with garrisons but never conquered it. The [[e:aztec-empire|Aztecs]] associated the Yopes with the god Xipe Totec, known as the Yopi god, whose priests wore the flayed skins of sacrificial victims. Its people spoke Tlapanec (Me'phaa).
yopitzinco.e: The Yopes fought the Spanish into the 1530s, revolting against colonial demands in 1531, before being subdued. The Me'phaa people and language survive in Guerrero.

yeke-kingdom.t: Msiri's trading kingdom in Katanga, a crossroads of copper, ivory and slave routes, ended by a Congo Free State expedition in 1891.
yeke-kingdom.o: Msiri, a Nyamwezi trader from western [[s:tanzania|Tanzania]], arrived in Katanga around 1856. By backing local factions against the [[s:kingdom-of-kazembe|Kingdom of Kazembe]] and the [[s:luba-empire|Luba Empire]], he made himself ruler, with his Yeke followers as the core of a new state centred on Bunkeya.
yeke-kingdom.r: Msiri's kingdom, known as Garanganze, controlled [[e:copper|copper]] mines and [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] to both the Atlantic and [[e:indian-ocean|Indian Ocean]] coasts. [[e:ovimbundu|Ovimbundu]] and [[e:swahili|Swahili]] traders brought guns and cloth in exchange for [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], copper and slaves. Msiri ruled through relatives, chiefs and warbands; the missionary Frederick Arnot settled at Bunkeya in 1886.
yeke-kingdom.e: In December 1891 Msiri was shot by Captain Omer Bodson of the Stairs Expedition, sent by the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]]. Katanga passed to the Free State, and his successor Mukanda-Bantu became a subordinate chief.

yenisei-kyrgyz-khaganate.t: A Turkic people of the upper Yenisei who destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate in 840 and briefly ruled the Mongolian steppe.
yenisei-kyrgyz-khaganate.o: The Kyrgyz of the Minusinsk basin on the upper Yenisei were known to Chinese sources for centuries, subject in turn to the Turkic [[e:khagan|khagans]] and the [[s:uyghur-khaganate|Uyghur Khaganate]]. After a long war, in 840 a Kyrgyz army allied with a dissident [[e:uyghurs|Uyghur]] general sacked Ordu-Baliq, scattering the Uyghurs.
yenisei-kyrgyz-khaganate.r: The Kyrgyz ruler, titled ajo or [[e:khagan|khagan]], ruled from the Yenisei and the Mongolian steppe, sending embassies to the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] court. The Kyrgyz combined herding, farming and iron working, and left many stelae in the Old Turkic runic script along the Yenisei. Chinese sources describe them as tall, with red hair and green eyes.
yenisei-kyrgyz-khaganate.e: The Kyrgyz never fully moved their centre to [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]]. In 924 the Khitan [[s:liao-dynasty|Liao dynasty]] drove them out of the Orkhon region, and they withdrew to the Yenisei. Their descendants are linked to the modern Kyrgyz and Khakas.

yaka-kingdom.t: A Lunda-founded kingdom on the Kwango river, ruled by the Kiamfu, which dominated the Yaka until Belgian conquest in 1906.
yaka-kingdom.o: In the 18th century [[e:lunda-empire|Lunda]] warriors from the east, moving out from the [[s:lunda-empire|Lunda Empire]], conquered the Yaka and other peoples of the middle Kwango valley. Their leader took the title Kiamfu and founded a kingdom centred at [[s:tippu-tips-state|Kasongo]] Lunda.
yaka-kingdom.r: The Kiamfu ruled through regional chiefs, many of [[e:lunda-empire|Lunda]] descent, who paid tribute in slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and [[e:raffia-cloth|raffia cloth]]. The kingdom acted as a middleman between the interior and Portuguese-linked traders in [[s:kingdom-of-kasanje|Kasanje]] and the [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kongo]] region. Yaka initiation rites and masks became widely known in African art.
yaka-kingdom.e: The [[e:congo-free-state|Congo Free State's]] forces fought the Kiamfu repeatedly in the 1890s and established control by 1906. The Kiamfu title survives as a customary office in the [[e:democratic-republic-of-the-congo|Democratic Republic of the Congo]].
